stages.name: Government intervention: subsidies
stages.title: Government intervention: subsidies
stages.sub: How a subsidy shifts the market, who gains, what it costs, and its trade-offs.

steps.q: A government pays bus firms £1 for every ticket sold, so it now costs the firm less to supply each ticket. If you drew this on a supply and demand diagram, which curve would move?
steps.right: The supply curve, to the right
steps.wrong: The demand curve, to the right
steps.hint: The payment lowers the firm's cost of supplying each ticket, not what buyers want to pay.

steps.q: Look at where the new supply curve crosses demand compared to the old crossing point. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
steps.hint: Supply has shifted right; trace the new equilibrium along the demand curve.

steps.q: The government pays £1 per ticket, and 2 million tickets are now sold. How would you work out the total amount the government hands over?
steps.right: Multiply the subsidy per unit by the new quantity sold
steps.wrong: Multiply the subsidy per unit by the old quantity sold
steps.hint: The government pays on every ticket actually sold after the subsidy, not before it.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: A vaccine creates benefits for people beyond the person vaccinated, so it is under-consumed at the market price. If a subsidy lowers its price and raises the quantity bought, what happens to those wider benefits?
steps.right: More of them are captured, since more people get vaccinated
steps.wrong: They stay the same, since only price has changed
steps.hint: Quantity bought rose. Does more of the good being consumed mean more of its third-party benefit is gained?

steps.q: A UK steel firm gets a subsidy that lets it lower its price without cutting its profit, while a foreign rival gets none. Whose steel looks cheaper to buyers now?
steps.hint: The subsidy let one firm cut its price without losing profit; the other firm's costs are unchanged.

steps.q: The money paid out on this subsidy could instead have built new hospital wards. Beyond the payment itself, what does the subsidy cost?
steps.right: The hospital wards that were given up
steps.wrong: The extra paperwork of paying it out
steps.hint: Think about what the same government money could have been spent on instead.
